blocks.text: A Turkish menu reads like a map. Many dishes carry the name of the town or city they come from, and each of those names is a compound noun of this unit: city + dish + `-(s)I`. *Adana kebabı* is a spicy minced-meat kebab from Adana, in the south; *Urfa kebabı*, from Şanlıurfa, is its milder neighbour. *İskender kebap*, thin slices of döner over bread with tomato sauce and yogurt, comes from Bursa, and the small meatballs of *İnegöl köftesi* from İnegöl, a town nearby. In Kayseri, in central Anatolia, the pride of the table is *mantı*: tiny dumplings under yogurt and melted butter, *Kayseri mantısı*.

**Gaziantep**, in the south-east near the Syrian border, has a reputation as one of Turkey's great food cities, and in 2015 UNESCO made it a Creative City of Gastronomy. Its best-known product is baklava: many thin layers of pastry, clarified butter, and the green pistachio of the region, *Antep fıstığı*. Since 2013 *Gaziantep baklavası*, also called *Antep baklavası*, has been a protected geographical indication in the European Union: only baklava made there, following agreed rules, may be sold under that name.

Further south, the province of **Hatay**, around ancient Antioch, joined UNESCO's network as a City of Gastronomy in 2017. Its cooking mixes Turkish and Arab traditions and counts hundreds of local dishes, and its signature dessert is *künefe*: shredded pastry baked around a soft, unsalted cheese and soaked in syrup, served hot. The earthquakes of 6 February 2023 destroyed many parts of Antakya, the provincial capital.

On the **Black Sea** coast, in the north, the star is a small fish, *hamsi*, the Black Sea anchovy, eaten fried or baked with rice. Corn goes into bread and many dishes, and the coast gives the country its tea, from the hills around Rize, and its hazelnuts, from Ordu and Giresun. Turkey grows more hazelnuts than any other country.

The **Aegean** coast, in the west, cooks with olive oil. The region grows about three quarters of Turkey's olives, and its best-loved dishes are the *zeytinyağlılar*, vegetables cooked slowly in olive oil and eaten cold. In spring, people gather wild herbs, *otlar*, from the hills; the town of Alaçatı near İzmir even holds a herb festival.
From east to west, the ingredients change but the table stays generous: a lentil soup, *mercimek çorbası*, a plate of something named after a town, and tea or a Turkish coffee to finish.

blocks.tr: Adana kebabı, İnegöl köftesi, Kayseri mantısı: bu yemeklerin adlarında bir şehir var. Antep baklavası ve Hatay künefesi de çok ünlü. Karadeniz'deki insanlar hamsiyi çok sever. Ege mutfağında zeytinyağı ve otlar çok önemli. Bugünkü menüde mercimek çorbası, Adana kebabı ve baklava var.
blocks.en: Adana kebab, İnegöl köfte, Kayseri mantı: there is a city in the names of these dishes. Antep baklava and Hatay künefe are very famous too. People on the Black Sea love hamsi. In Aegean cooking, olive oil and herbs are very important. On today's menu there are lentil soup, Adana kebab and baklava.

vocab.en: künefe, a hot cheese pastry in syrup

questions.q: Which city became a UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy in 2015?
In the Turkish text, what does *Karadeniz'deki insanlar* mean?
options: the people on the Black Sea
the Black Sea's people are in
questions.explain: *Karadeniz'de* + *-ki*: an adjective, **the people (who are) on the Black Sea**.
A compound named after the city: a kind of *mantı*, not one owned by anyone.

sources.title: Turkish cuisine
sources.note: Specialties often named for places; Urfa kebap less spicy than Adana kebap; İskender from Bursa; İnegöl köftesi; mantı associated with Kayseri; Black Sea cooking uses fish, especially hamsi, and maize; olive oil as the main cooking oil in the west; the south-east known for kebabs, baklava and künefe
